T2 Mac Wi-Fi & Bluetooth guide

apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher on Omarchy

Pull your T2 Mac's Wi-Fi and Bluetooth firmware straight off macOS — one install, one run.

Reviewed 2026-11-17 · independent editorial guide

Short answer

Install apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher with omarchy pkg add apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher, run the fetcher once to copy the firmware from your macOS volume to /lib/firmware/brcm, and reboot — Wi-Fi and Bluetooth come up. Note: the exact run command is still unverified; use pacman -Ql to find the installed script.

On this page Install Getting started Common issues Comparison Questions

apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher on Omarchy

apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher is a tiny one-shot tool for T2 Macs running Omarchy: it pulls the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth firmware for your Broadcom chip straight off the macOS install still on your disk, so your wireless works without ever booting back into macOS to run scripts by hand.

TL;DR

omarchy pkg add apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher
pacman -Ql apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher   # find the installed script — see note below
sudo <the installed fetcher script>     # pick "Retrieve the firmware directly from macOS"

It takes ~1 minute (9.3 KB download, 14.5 KB installed). Then run the fetcher once — it mounts your macOS volume, copies the firmware to /lib/firmware/brcm, and reloads the drivers.

Exact run command — unverified, read this first. The store page documents the install command but not what to run afterwards, and no public PKGBUILD for this package could be found to check against. The package is far too small (14.5 KB installed) to contain the full t2linux firmware.sh, so it ships a wrapper of some kind. Until someone runs pacman -Ql apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher on a real T2 install and records the exact command, use that listing to find the script and run it with sudo, choosing option 2 ("Retrieve the firmware directly from macOS") when it asks. That is the top item on the verify checklist above.

Getting started (5 minutes)

0. Before you run it — check you qualify.

This tool only works if macOS is still on your disk (a dual-boot setup). It reads the firmware from your macOS volume; if you wiped macOS entirely, this package cannot help you — method 5 in the comparison table below is the only option then. It also does not work on iMac19,1, iMac19,2, or iMacPro1,1 (the wiki says methods 4 and 5 don't work for those models — you need methods 1–3). And you probably need internet on Linux for the first run: the fetcher needs an APFS driver to read the macOS volume, and if it isn't already installed it downloads and builds one — use Ethernet, USB tethering from your phone, or an external USB Wi-Fi adapter to get online first, since your built-in Wi-Fi is exactly what's broken.

Quick pre-flight checks:

uname -r            # you should be on a linux-t2 kernel (see linux-t2 below)
lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE | grep -i apfs   # you should see an APFS partition (usually nvme0n1p2)

1. Install.

One command from any terminal:

omarchy pkg add apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher

Confirm it landed: pacman -Qi apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher should show version 1-2.

2. Run the fetcher.

Find what it installed (pacman -Ql apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher), then run that script with sudo and choose option 2, "Retrieve the firmware directly from macOS". Under the hood it does the t2linux wiki's method 4 for you:

  • Loads the APFS driver (linux-apfs-rw) so Linux can read the macOS volume — installing it from the AUR first if it's missing, which is the step that needs internet and kernel headers.
  • Mounts the macOS APFS partition (it tries the volumes on your NVMe drive until it finds one containing /usr/share/firmware).
  • Extracts and renames the firmware for your exact chip (BCM4355, BCM4364, or BCM4377 — the script knows which files your model needs) and copies them to /lib/firmware/brcm.
  • Reloads the drivers: brcmfmac (Wi-Fi) and hci_bcm4377 (Bluetooth).

3. Verify it worked.

Check the kernel log for the firmware actually loading:

sudo journalctl -k --grep=brcmfmac

You want to see a line like Firmware: BCM4377/4 wl0: ... version 16.20.328.0.3.6.105 and your interface renamed to something like wlp1s0f0. Don't panic about lines saying Direct firmware load for brcm/brcmfmac4377b3-pcie.apple,...bin failed with error -2 — the driver tries several board-specific filenames before it finds the right one, and the wiki's own example log is full of those -2 lines before the successful load. They only matter if no firmware line follows them. Then check Wi-Fi shows up (ip link should list a wireless interface) and Bluetooth (bluetoothctl list should show a controller). If nothing appears, a reboot is the cheap next step before digging into the issues below.

The 3 things you need to know:

  • It's a one-shot tool, not an app. There is no window, no service, no config file, and nothing in ~/.config. You run it once (and again after macOS updates — see below), it does its job, and it's done. If you want it gone afterwards, omarchy pkg drop apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher removes it; the firmware files it placed in /lib/firmware/brcm stay put, which is what you want.
  • The firmware comes from YOUR macOS install. Apple doesn't license this firmware for redistribution, which is why there's no linux-firmware package for it and why this tool extracts it from the copy of macOS already on your machine. Keep a macOS partition around — even a small one — or the fetcher has nothing to read from.
  • Re-run it after macOS updates. A macOS update can ship newer firmware files, and the files in /lib/firmware/brcm are just a snapshot of whatever macOS had when you last ran the fetcher. After a macOS update, run it again to pick up the new files, then reload the drivers (the script does that part for you).

Config location.

None — this is a run-once script, not a service. Everything it produces lives in /lib/firmware/brcm (the firmware files themselves, e.g. brcmfmac4377b3-pcie.bin, .clm_blob, .txt, and Bluetooth brcmbt*.bin/.ptb files).

Common issues & fixes

All of these come from the t2linux wiki's Wi-Fi/Bluetooth guide and the firmware.sh source itself — they are the project's documented failure modes, not guesses. Each one is still marked for on-machine confirmation in the checklist above.

"Could not find location of firmware. Aborting!"

The fetcher mounts the APFS volumes, finds no /usr/share/firmware anywhere, and gives up. The usual cause is that macOS is gone — you wiped the macOS partition when installing Linux, or the macOS volume is on a different disk than the script expects (it looks at the nvme0n1 drive).

Fix: Check whether a macOS volume exists at all:

lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE,SIZE | grep -i apfs

If nothing shows up, macOS is gone and this package cannot work for you — the wiki is explicit: if you removed macOS after installing Linux, method 5 is the only option. That means running the full firmware.sh yourself and choosing "Download a macOS Recovery Image from Apple" (see the comparison table). If an APFS partition does show up but the fetcher still can't find the firmware, your macOS install may be too old or damaged — same fallback applies.

The APFS driver won't install or load

The fetcher needs the linux-apfs-rw kernel module to read the macOS volume, and it isn't installed. On Arch-based systems the script builds it from the AUR (linux-apfs-rw-dkms-git), which needs git, base-devel, kernel headers, and internet. If any of those is missing, the install fails with "APFS driver could not be loaded" and the script exits.

Fix: Get online first (Ethernet or USB tethering — your built-in Wi-Fi can't help yet), then make sure the build tools and headers are present:

sudo pacman -Sy --noconfirm git base-devel linux-t2-headers

Then run the fetcher again. If it still fails, reboot and try once more — the wiki's own advice for a stubborn APFS install is to restart the Mac and run the script again. If the driver loads but the mount still fails and your macOS volume has FileVault turned on, that may be the wall: linux-apfs-rw has no encryption support, and T2 hardware-encrypted volumes can't be unlocked from Linux even with the recovery key (per the APFS driver docs and Arch forum reports on this exact scenario). Unverified for this package's flow — the wiki doesn't call FileVault out for method 4 — but if you hit it, the fallback is method 5 (Recovery image), which doesn't need to mount your disk at all.

Wi-Fi works, but Bluetooth doesn't (or vice versa)

One radio comes up and the other doesn't. The most common cause is the macOS version your firmware came from: on MacBookPro15,4, MacBookPro16,3, and MacBookAir9,1, Bluetooth firmware only exists on macOS Monterey or later — if your macOS install is older than Monterey, the script copies Wi-Fi firmware only and warns you about it. The other common cause is the Bluetooth driver simply not reloading after the files land.

Fix: First, reload the Bluetooth driver by hand:

sudo modprobe -r hci_bcm4377
sudo modprobe hci_bcm4377

Then check bluetoothctl list shows a controller. If it's still missing and your macOS is older than Monterey, update macOS to Monterey or later and re-run the fetcher — or use method 5 with a Monterey-or-later Recovery image, which the wiki says gives complete firmware files. If Wi-Fi is the one that's missing instead, reload its driver the same way (sudo modprobe -r brcmfmac && sudo modprobe brcmfmac) and check the journal (sudo journalctl -k --grep=brcmfmac) for the firmware line.

Firmware loads, but Wi-Fi still won't connect

The firmware is in place, the interface exists, networks appear — but connecting fails even with the right password. This is a known regression, not a firmware problem: since wpa_supplicant 2.11, Wi-Fi on Broadcom chips is broken. The t2linux wiki flags it at the top of the Wi-Fi guide.

Fix: Switch your Wi-Fi backend to iwd, or disable offloading by adding brcmfmac.feature_disable=0x82000 to your kernel parameters. The wiki notes this currently affects Arch Linux and EndeavourOS. Also check you're not using the broadcom-wl driver — the wiki is blunt about this: broadcom-wl is not the driver for these Macs, brcmfmac (in the kernel) is the only one that supports them, and a lot of "Wi-Fi not working" reports turn out to be people on broadcom-wl. If you installed it, remove it.

The fetcher does nothing on an iMac19,1, iMac19,2, or iMacPro1,1

You're on one of these three models and method 4 silently can't work for you. The wiki states it plainly: for iMac19,1, iMac19,2, and iMacPro1,1, methods 4 and 5 will not work — you must choose a method from 1–3. (These are the non-T2 iMacs the guide also covers, and their firmware needs extra NVRAM/TxCap files the direct-from-macOS path doesn't fetch.)

Fix: Don't fight the fetcher — use the full firmware.sh instead. Boot into macOS, download the script from the wiki, run it there, and pick method 1 (copy firmware to the EFI partition), method 2 (tarball), or method 3 (build a Linux package). Method 1 needs no extra software on macOS, so it's the simplest if you don't want to install Homebrew tools. Full steps are in the wiki guide linked in Sources.

Pairs well with / If you hate this, try

Pairs well with

  • linux-t2 — the T2 kernel and modules this firmware is for; without the T2 kernel's brcmfmac support the firmware has nothing to load into, so install the kernel first if you haven't. apple-t2-audio-config — the ALSA config for the T2 audio driver, the next "why doesn't my hardware work" fix after Wi-Fi. t2fanrd — fan control for T2 Macs, since a Linux install with no fan curve will cook itself quietly while you're celebrating the Wi-Fi working.

If you hate this, try

  • The full firmware.sh from the t2linux wiki, run by hand — same script, all five methods, including the ones this package doesn't cover (EFI copy, tarball, package build, Recovery image download). It's the fallback for every case above where this package can't help: macOS wiped, iMac19,1/19,2/iMacPro1,1, or FileVault trouble. Or a $10–15 USB Wi-Fi adapter as a stopgap while you sort the firmware out — it gets you online for the APFS driver download, and it's the thing the wiki itself suggests keeping handy.

Verdict: If macOS is still on your disk and you're on a T2 Mac (not one of the three iMacs), this package is the obvious pick — it's the same script the wiki tells you to run, minus the manual download and the menu. If macOS is gone, skip it entirely and go straight to method 5. If you're on iMac19,1/19,2/iMacPro1,1, methods 1–3 are your only options.

There is no paid product to replace here

There is no paid product to replace here, and the guide won't pretend otherwise. The firmware is Apple's proprietary blob — you already own it as part of the Mac you bought, and this package just extracts it from your own disk instead of making you run the wiki's script by hand. The honest framing is time, not money: the manual path (download firmware.sh, read the wiki, pick a method, build an APFS driver from the AUR) is free too, and it works fine — this package just compresses it into one install command and one run. What you give up for that convenience: the other four methods. If method 4 can't work for your machine, the manual script is the answer, not a different app.

Frequently asked questions

Does apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher work on Omarchy?

Yes — it's in the official Omarchy repo as apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher (version 1-2, added Nov 16, 2026) and installs with one command: omarchy pkg add apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher. It's a 9.3 KB download. Note the exact command to run after installing is still unverified (see the TL;DR note) — use pacman -Ql apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher to find the installed script.

What if I erased macOS entirely?

This package can't help you — it reads firmware from the macOS volume on your disk, and there's nothing to read. Use method 5 from the t2linux wiki: run the full firmware.sh and choose "Download a macOS Recovery Image from Apple", picking a macOS version between Monterey and Sonoma for complete firmware files. You'll need internet on Linux (Ethernet or USB tethering).

Is the firmware free / open source?

The package is MIT-licensed and free. The firmware is not open source — it's Apple's proprietary Broadcom firmware, and the reason this tooling exists is that Apple doesn't redistribute it. You extract it from the macOS install you already own, which is the arrangement the t2linux project documents. Don't go looking for a downloadable firmware package for these chips; that's the whole point of the fetcher.

Do I need internet to run it?

Possibly. The fetcher needs an APFS driver to read the macOS volume, and if it isn't already on your system the script installs it from the AUR — which needs internet, git, base-devel, and kernel headers. If your T2 install already has the driver (e.g. it shipped with your install media), no internet is needed. Either way, have Ethernet or phone USB tethering ready before you start, since built-in Wi-Fi is down until the firmware lands.

Does it work on Apple Silicon Macs?

No. This is for Intel Macs with the T2 security chip (2018–2020 MacBook Pro/Air, Mac mini, iMac Pro, and related models), plus the iMac19,1/19,2 exceptions — which, confusingly, this method does not cover. Apple Silicon Macs are a different project entirely (Asahi Linux) and this package is irrelevant there.

Why is there no app icon or window?

Because there's nothing to launch — it's a run-once script, not a program. Install it, run it, confirm Wi-Fi works, and optionally remove it (omarchy pkg drop apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher). The firmware files stay in /lib/firmware/brcm either way.

Do I have to re-run it after updates?

After a macOS update, yes — re-run it so /lib/firmware/brcm picks up any newer firmware macOS shipped. After a Linux kernel update, no — the firmware files persist, though a reboot is needed for the new kernel to load them. If Wi-Fi breaks after a kernel update, reload the modules (sudo modprobe -r brcmfmac && sudo modprobe brcmfmac) before assuming the firmware is gone.

How do I uninstall it?

omarchy pkg drop apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher. That removes the fetcher script; it does not remove the firmware files from /lib/firmware/brcm, so your Wi-Fi keeps working.
